prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: Topological insulators introduced a genuinely new classification of band insulators, the Z2 invariant, with protected edge and surface states that follow from band structure and symmetry rather than from fine-tuning. The Kane-Mele papers gave the theory, and Molenkamp's group observed the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe wells soon after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The field is mature: it has been confirmed in many materials and probes, and it has changed how first-principles electronic-structure work is done, since topological invariants are now routinely computed with DFT and used to screen materials. It is also a clean theory-plus-experiment pairing that fits a three-person prize. Five of eight members rank it in their top three, which is broad support from members whose own fields differ.
statement.case_against: Credit is contested. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe case, Fu, Kane and Mele the three-dimensional case, and Hasan's and others' ARPES work established the 3D materials, so a three-name prize leaves out real contributors. It is also unclear how central the quantum spin Hall effect is compared with 3D topological insulators, and practical applications remain largely prospective. Optical lattice clocks (B057) have a clearer discovery-plus-invention profile and a more concrete present-day impact on metrology.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks (B057) first and topological insulators second, arguing that the clocks reach 1e-18 and open geodesy, tests of constants and a redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that B057 is strong and I rank it fourth, so this is not a dispute about worthiness. My reservation is that the lattice clock is the culmination of a longer line, with frequency combs and ion clocks already recognised, so the distinct step credited to Katori and Ye needs careful framing. Topological insulators opened a new organising principle for a whole field rather than improving a measurement. I would still accept B057 as a good outcome if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Puts B057 first as a discovery-plus-invention, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B015) second as a rapidly adopted field-opening result.
responses.response: I accept the metrology argument but disagree on B015 versus B053. Twisted bilayer graphene is exciting, but the nature of the superconductivity is still debated and the experimental field is under ten years old. Topological insulators have been tested across many materials and techniques for about fifteen years, with a stable interpretation. That difference in maturity is why I place B053 ahead.

responses.point: Ranks the cavity method (B025) first and argues it gave a controlled statistical-physics framework for constraint satisfaction, coding and inference.
responses.response: The cavity method is deep and its link to spin glasses is real, but I am uneasy about treating results whose main impact lies in computer science and inference as the leading physics discovery of this cycle. Only one member ranks it at all, so it has not been tested against the committee. I would want an argument that its physical content, not its algorithmic reach, is the point before moving it up. I note that you also rank B053 third, so we overlap there.

responses.point: Ranks IceCube neutrinos (B054) first as a new observational window led by Halzen, Karle and Spiering, with topological insulators second.
responses.response: I take the new-window argument seriously, and neutrino astronomy is a real discovery. My concern is attribution: IceCube is a large collaboration, and the diffuse flux, blazar association and Galactic plane results are collaboration results with analysis leaders outside the credit, so a three-name prize is harder to defend than for B053. I would like to hear from the astrophysics-oriented members whether the three names capture the decisive contributions.

responses.point: Ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B048) first as an invention that overcame a limit recognised since Scherzer.
responses.response: B048 is a clean invention and the three names match the corrector story well. I did not rank it on my opening ballot, so I have not weighed it closely, but I would ask how much of its weight is as an instrument versus a discovery in physics. That is a qualification rather than an objection, since the prize has honoured instrumentation before.

uncertainties: Whether Hasan should be included for the 3D ARPES work, which would require dropping one of the three names.
Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are essential to the HgTe link, or whether quantum spin Hall plus Z2 topological insulators can be treated as one achievement with the proposed three names.
Whether B057 should be treated as the clear first choice given its three first-place rankings, and how the earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes bear on its novelty.
How much weight to give B026 given the 2007 GMR prize, since only I rank it first.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B053. My field is first-principles electronic-structure theory and magnetism at Uppsala, so B026 (tunnel magnetoresistance) and B053 sit close to my research area, which is scientific proximity rather than a documented personal or institutional connection to any named candidate.
